messages.author: 2cad44f9d2d01bcb
messages.subject: modelled occurrence as a covariate
parts:
Hi Group,


I am estimating occupancy and abundance (using RN model) for several wild ungulate species in Lao PDR. During the survey we also collected data on threats (presence of domestic livestock, presence of snares, and presence of humans) which are predicted to be major determinants of ungulate occurrence/abundance.


Threats are also detected imperfectly so conceptually what I need is two-species co-occurrence model (which makes sense when thinking wild deer and domestic cattle, maybe less so when thinking about wild deer and snares, or humans!). Such models (i.e. Mackenzie et al. 2004) aren’t implemented in unmarked and though at a later date I will look at this in BUGS, I need something quick in the meantime.


Could I just estimate psi for each of the threats, use those values as a covariates in my species models, and then use AIC as normal to test for evidence that they are important predictors of occurrence/abundance? Or is that statistically non-allowable “double-dipping”?


I have some memory of a similar discussion in this forum but I wasn’t able to find it. Apologies if this topic has been dealt with before.


Hannah

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: modelled occurrence as a covariate
parts:
Hi Hannah,

FWIW: Link (1999) offers some perspective.   I would think that if p-star is really high for cattle or people, using psi-hat cow or psi-hat person (or observed cow or human presence for that matter) might be reasonably approximate.  Not to betray 'unmarked' or anything, but you can fit MacKenzie's 2004 model (and Richmond's more stable 2010 model) in MARK/PRESENCE, so if that's the sort of model you want to evaluate, you may not need to be approximate.  

That said, there are plenty of examples where a detection index for one species is used as a predictor for another.

messages.author: 2cad44f9d2d01bcb
messages.subject: Re: modelled occurrence as a covariate
parts: Thanks for the comments and for the reference John. My rationale for using estimated psi is that it just seems intuitively nonsensical to use observed presence of cattle/people/hunting etc when I am implicitly acknowledging that these data may be a poor representation of the real occurrence of these threats.  And I do appreciate that more explicit co-occurrence models can be fit elsewhere but in the immediate term I need to find a way of presenting the analysis of these, and other, data within one relatively user-friendly environment, and for various reasons that is going to be unmarked.

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] modelled occurrence as a covariate
parts:
hi Hannah,
 I think if you have a large data set then using psi-hat for one species as a covariate for the other is not a terrible thing to do and should not be too misleading. That said, it would be preferable to do the joint model. This is one area we hope to improve unmarked in over the next year or two (first, dynamic models.....). We will see where things go.
regards
andy

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] modelled occurrence as a covariate
parts:
We should also point out that psi-hat for a given threat needs to vary by site in order to be useful.  Maybe this is obvious, but you'll want covariates associated with the presence or detection of the threat so that your first round model has a predicted psi-hat for each site.

The other option is to use ranef() to get you the latent occurrence state for the threat, which is really what you are trying to model.  It is still useful to have covariates that can discriminate between sites but in the case of a null "fm_threat" model, you could use the mean latent states to generate random values and serve as the covariate for sites without detections, increasing the uncertainty of estimated relationships:

threat_site <- rbinom(n.sites, 1, bup(ranef(fm_threat), stat="mean"))

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] modelled occurrence as a covariate
parts:
Dan makes some good points here -- and I agree when the model you're thinking about involves the latent state variables then you should use the estimated occupancy state as the covariate.
Note: in the context of spatial models of occupancy where z[site] is influenced by z[neighboring sites] then you can implement a kind of iterative procedure where you estimate the true occupancy state, use that as a covariate to estimate the parameters of the model, then update the predictions of z, repeat a few times.
 
We will cover this in some later chapter of Volume 2 of the AHM book.
 
Also Nichols and others have done this kind of thing in several papers which I don't have at the tip of my fingers here (maybe some spotted owl papers). If someone has a reference or two to offer up please do.
